children.translated_text: Having placed <s>Viśveśa</s> in his heart and having performed reverence to the teacher,
the <s>Tarkasaṃgraha</s> is composed for the easy understanding of children.
The seven <s>padārthas</s> (categories) are substance, quality, action, universal, particularity, inherence, and absence.
Among these, the substances are exactly nine: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, direction, self, and mind.

The twenty-four qualities are color, taste, smell, touch, number, measure, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, nearness, heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, sound, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and disposition.
The five actions are upward motion, downward motion, contraction, expansion, and movement.
The universal is of two kinds: higher and lower.
The particularities, which reside in eternal substances, are indeed infinite.
Inherence, however, is only one.
Absence is fourfold:
prior absence, posterior absence, absolute absence, and mutual absence.
Earth is that which possesses smell.
It is of two kinds, eternal and non-eternal.
The eternal is in the form of atoms.
The non-eternal is in the form of effects.
Again, it is threefold by the distinction of body, sense-organ, and object.
The body is that of people such as ourselves.
The sense-organ is the nose, the apprehender of smell, situated at the tip of the nose.
The object is clay, stone, and the like.
Water is that which possesses cold touch.
It is of two kinds, eternal and non-eternal.
The eternal waters are in the form of atoms.
The non-eternal waters are in the form of effects.
Again, they are threefold by the distinction of body, sense-organ, and object.
The body exists in the world of <s>Varuṇa</s>.
The sense-organ is the tongue, the apprehender of taste, situated at the tip of the tongue.
The object is a river, ocean, and the like.
Fire is that which possesses hot touch.
It is of two kinds, eternal and non-eternal.
The eternal is in the form of atoms.
The non-eternal is in the form of effects.
Again, it is threefold by the distinction of body, sense-organ, and object.
The body exists in the solar world.
The sense-organ is the eye, the apprehender of color, situated at the front of the black pupil.
The object is fourfold,
by the distinction of terrestrial, celestial, gastric, and mineral-born.
The terrestrial is fire and the like.
The celestial, not dependent on fuel, is lightning and the like.
The gastric is the cause of the transformation of what has been eaten; the mineral-born is gold and the like.
Air is that which has touch but is devoid of color.
It is of two kinds, eternal and non-eternal.
The eternal is in the form of atoms.
The non-eternal is in the form of effects.
Again, it is threefold by the distinction of body, sense-organ, and object.
The body exists in the world of air.
The sense-organ is the skin, the apprehender of touch, pervading the whole body.
The object is the cause of trembling in trees and the like.
The air that moves inside the body is <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath).
And although it is one, because of differences in limiting conditions it receives names such as <s>prāṇa</s> and <s>apāna</s>.
Ether is that whose quality is sound.
And it is one, all-pervading, and eternal.
Time is the cause of practical usage concerning past and so forth.
And it is one, all-pervading, and eternal.
Direction is the cause of practical usage concerning east and so forth.
And it is one, all-pervading, and eternal.
The self is the substrate of cognition.
It is twofold: the supreme self and the individual self.
Among these, the Lord, omniscient, is the one supreme self.

children.text: jīvātmā pratiśarīraṃ bhinno vibhur nityaś ca ||
children.translated_text: The individual self is different in each body, and is all-pervading and eternal.
Mind is the sense-organ that is the means for the apprehension of pleasure and the like.

children.text: tac ca pratyātmaniyatatvād anantaṃ paramāṇurūpaṃ nityaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: And because it is restricted to each self, it is infinite in number, atomic in form, and eternal.
Color is a quality apprehended by the eye alone.
It is sevenfold by the distinctions white, blue, yellow, red, green, tawny, and variegated, and it resides in earth, water, and fire.
Among these, in earth it is sevenfold.
In water there is non-luminous white.
In fire there is luminous white.
Taste is a quality apprehended by the tongue.
It is sixfold by the distinctions sweet, sour, salty, pungent, astringent, and bitter.
In earth it is sixfold.
In water it is only sweet.
Smell is a quality apprehended by the nose.
It is of two kinds, fragrant and foul.
It resides only in earth.
Touch is a quality apprehended only by the sense-organ of the skin.
It is threefold by the distinctions cold, hot, and neither hot nor cold.
It resides in earth, water, fire, and air.
Among these, cold touch is in water.
Hot touch is in fire.
Neither-hot-nor-cold touch is in earth and air.
The group of four beginning with color in earth is produced by cooking and is non-eternal.
Elsewhere it is not produced by cooking, and is eternal or ultimate.
What is present in an eternal thing is eternal.
What is present in a non-eternal thing is non-eternal.
Number is the cause of practical usage such as unity.
It resides in the nine substances and extends from oneness up to the highest number.
Oneness is eternal and non-eternal.
What is present in an eternal thing is eternal; what is present in a non-eternal thing is non-eternal.
But duality and the rest are everywhere only non-eternal.
Measure is the cause of practical usage concerning measuring.
It resides in the nine substances.
It is fourfold:
minute, great, long, and short.
Separateness is the cause of practical usage concerning being separate.
It resides in all substances.
Conjunction is the cause of practical usage concerning being conjoined.
It resides in all substances.
Disjunction is the quality that destroys conjunction.
It resides in all substances.
Remoteness and nearness are the special causes of practical usages of farther and nearer.
They reside in the four beginning with earth and in mind, so it is said.
They are of two kinds: produced by direction and produced by time.
In what is distant, remoteness is produced by direction.
In what is near, nearness is produced by direction.
In what is older, remoteness is produced by time.
In what is younger, nearness is produced by time.
Heaviness is the non-inherent cause of the first falling.
It resides in earth and water.
Fluidity is the non-inherent cause of the first flowing, and it resides in earth, water, and fire.
That is twofold: natural and occasional.
Natural liquidity exists in water; occasional liquidity exists in earth and fire.
In earth, liquidity is found in things such as ghee, produced by contact with fire.
In fire, it is found in things such as gold.
Viscidity is the quality that causes powders and the like to become a lump.
It occurs only in water.
Sound is a quality apprehended by the ear.
It occurs only in ether.
It is twofold: of the nature of noise and of the nature of phonemes.
That which is of the nature of noise occurs in drums and the like.
That which is of the nature of phonemes has the form of Sanskrit speech and the like.
Cognition, which is the cause of all practical activity, is knowledge.
It is twofold: memory and experience.
Knowledge produced solely from an impression is memory.
Knowledge other than that is experience.
That is twofold: veridical and non-veridical.
An experience whose mode corresponds to a thing possessing that mode is veridical.

children.text: yathā rajata idaṃ rajatam iti jñānam
children.translated_text: For example, with regard to silver, the cognition 'this is silver.'
That very cognition is called <s>pramā</s> (valid cognition).
An experience whose mode is applied to something lacking that mode is non-veridical.

children.text: yathā śuktāv idaṃ rajatam iti jñānam ||
children.translated_text: For example, with regard to mother-of-pearl, the cognition 'this is silver.'
Veridical experience is fourfold, divided into perception, inferential cognition, analogical cognition, and verbal cognition.
Its instrument too is fourfold, divided into perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony.
The extraordinary cause is the instrument.
A cause is that which invariably precedes an effect.
An effect is the counterpositive of a prior absence.
Cause is threefold, divided into inherent, non-inherent, and instrumental causes.

children.text: yat samavetaṃ kāryam utpadyate tat samavāyikāraṇam
children.translated_text: That in which the effect arises by inherence is the inherent cause.

children.text: yathā tantavaḥ paṭasya paṭaś ca khagatarūpādeḥ
children.translated_text: For example, the threads are the inherent cause of cloth, and cloth is the inherent cause of the color and so on belonging to the cloth.

children.text: kāryeṇa kāraṇena vā sahaikasminn arthe samavetatve sati yat kāraṇaṃ tad asamavāyikāraṇam
children.translated_text: When a cause inheres in one and the same entity together with the effect or together with the cause, that is a non-inherent cause.
For example, the conjunction of threads is the non-inherent cause of cloth, and the color of the threads is the non-inherent cause of the color of the cloth.
A cause different from both of those is the instrumental cause.
For example, the shuttle, loom, and the like are instrumental causes of cloth.

children.text: tad etattrividhakāraṇamadhye yad asādhāraṇaṃ kāraṇaṃ tad eva karaṇam ||
children.translated_text: Among these three kinds of cause, whatever is the extraordinary cause, that alone is the instrument.
Among these, perception is the instrument of perceptual cognition.
Perception is knowledge produced by the contact of a sense faculty with an object.
It is twofold: indeterminate and determinate.

children.text: tatra nirvikalpakaṃ jñānaṃ nirvikalpakaṃ yathedaṃ kiṃcit
children.translated_text: Among these, indeterminate cognition is indeterminate, as in 'this is something.'

children.text: saparakārakaṃ jñānaṃ savikalpakaṃ yathā ḍittho'yam brahmaṇo 'yaṃ śyāmo'yam iti ||
children.translated_text: Cognition with qualifiers is determinate, as in 'this is <s>Ḍittha</s>,' 'this is a Brahmin,' or 'this is dark.'
The contact between sense faculty and object, the cause of perceptual cognition, is sixfold.

children.text: saṃyogaḥ saṃyuktasamavāyaḥ saṃyuktasamavetasamavāyaḥ samavāyaḥ samavetasamavāyo viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvaś ceti
children.translated_text: They are conjunction, inherence in what is conjoined, inherence in what inheres in what is conjoined, inherence, inherence in what inheres, and the relation of qualifier and qualificand.
In producing visual perception of a pot by the eye, conjunction is the contact.

children.text: ghaṭarūpapratyakṣajanane saṃyuktasamavāyaḥ sannikarṣaḥ cakṣuḥsaṃyukte ghaṭe rūpasya samavāyāt
children.translated_text: In producing perception of the color of a pot, inherence in what is conjoined is the contact, because color inheres in the pot conjoined with the eye.

children.text: rūpatvasāmānyapratyakṣe saṃyuktasamavetasamavāyaḥ sannikarṣaḥ cakṣuḥsaṃyukte ghaṭe rūpaṃ samavetaṃ tatra rūpatvasya samavāyāt
children.translated_text: In the perception of the universal colorhood, inherence in what inheres in what is conjoined is the contact, because color inheres in the pot conjoined with the eye, and colorhood inheres in that color.
By the ear, because sound is a quality of ether and because there is inherence between a quality and the possessor of the quality.

children.text: śabdatvasākṣātkāre samavetasamavāyaḥ sannikarṣaḥ śrotrasamavete śabde śabdatvasya samavāyāt
children.translated_text: In the direct apprehension of soundhood, inherence in what inheres is the contact, because soundhood inheres in sound, which inheres in the ear.

children.text: abhāvapratyakṣe viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvaḥ sannikarṣo ghaṭābhāvavad bhṛtalam ity atra cakṣuḥsaṃyukte bhūtale ghaṭābhāvasya viśeṣaṇatvāt
children.translated_text: In the perception of absence, the relation of qualifier and qualificand is the contact; in the expression 'the ground has the absence of a pot,' the absence of the pot is a qualifier of the ground conjoined with the eye.
Thus knowledge produced by the six kinds of contact is perception.
Its instrument is the sense faculty.
Therefore it is established that the sense faculty is the means of perceptual knowledge.
Inference is the instrument of inferential cognition.
Knowledge produced from reflective consideration is inferential cognition.
Reflective consideration is knowledge that the subject possesses a property qualified by pervasion.

children.text: yathā vahnivyāpyadhūmavān ayaṃ parvata iti jñānaṃ parāmarśaḥ
children.translated_text: For example, the cognition 'this mountain has smoke pervaded by fire' is reflective consideration.

children.text: taj janyaṃ parvato vahnimān iti jñānam anumitiḥ
children.translated_text: The cognition produced from that, 'the mountain has fire,' is inferential cognition.

children.text: yatra yatra dhūmas tatrāgnir iti sāhacaryaniyamo vyāptiḥ
children.translated_text: The invariable concomitance 'wherever there is smoke, there is fire' is pervasion.
The occurrence of the pervaded property in a mountain and the like is subjecthood.
Inference is twofold: for oneself and for another.
Among these, inference for oneself is the cause of one's own inferential cognition.

children.text: tathā hi svayam eva bhūyo darśanena yatra dhūmas tatra agnir iti mahānasādau vyāptiṃ gṛhītvā parvatasamīpaṃ gatas tadgate cāgnau saṃdihānaḥ parvate dhūmaṃ paśyan vyāptiṃ smarati yatra dhūmas tatrāgnir iti
children.translated_text: Thus, after one has oneself, through repeated observation, grasped the pervasion 'where there is smoke, there is fire' in a kitchen and the like, and has gone near a mountain while doubting whether there is fire there, seeing smoke on the mountain one remembers the pervasion, 'where there is smoke, there is fire.'

children.text: tadantaraṃ vahnivyāpyadhūmavān ayaṃ parvata iti jñānam utpadyate
children.translated_text: Immediately afterward there arises the cognition 'this mountain has smoke pervaded by fire.'
This very thing is called consideration of the inferential mark.

children.text: tasmāt parvato vahnimān iti jñānam anumitir utpadyate
children.translated_text: From that, the inferential cognition 'the mountain has fire' arises.
This is inference for oneself.

children.text: yat tu svayaṃ dhūmād agnim anumāya parapratipattyarthaṃ pañcāvayavavākyaṃ prayukte tat parārthānumānam
children.translated_text: But when, after oneself inferring fire from smoke, one uses a five-membered statement for the understanding of another, that is inference for another.
For example: the mountain has fire, because it has smoke.

children.text: yo yo dhūmavān sa vahnimān yathā mahānasaḥ
children.translated_text: Whatever has smoke has fire, as a kitchen does.
And this is so.
Therefore it is so.
Through the inferential mark presented by this statement, another person too understands the fire.
The proposition, reason, example, application, and conclusion are the five members.
'The mountain has fire' is the proposition.
'Because it has smoke' is the reason.

children.text: yo yo dhūmavān sa so'gnimān yathā mahānasa ity udāharaṇam
children.translated_text: The example is: 'Whoever possesses smoke possesses fire, as in a kitchen.'
'And so this is such' is the application.
'Therefore it is such' is the conclusion.
For inference for oneself and inference for another, reflection on the mark alone is the instrument.
Therefore inference is reflection on the mark.
The mark is threefold.
It is positive-and-negative, purely positive, and purely negative.
That which has pervasion through positive concomitance and through negative concomitance is positive-and-negative.
For example, when fire is to be proved, the possession of smoke.

children.text: yatra dhūmas tatrāgnir yathā mahānasa ity anvayavyāptiḥ
children.translated_text: 'Where there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen' is positive pervasion.

children.text: yatra vahnir nāsti tatra dhūmo'pi nāsti yathā mahāhrada iti vyatirekavyāptiḥ
children.translated_text: 'Where there is no fire, there is also no smoke, as in a great lake' is negative pervasion.

children.text: anvayamātravyāptikaṃ kevalānvayi yathā ghaṭo'bhidheyaḥ prameyatvāt paṭavat
children.translated_text: That whose pervasion is only positive is purely positive, as in: 'A pot is nameable, because it is knowable, like a cloth.'

children.text: atra prameyatvābhidhyatvayor vyatirekavyāptir nāsti sarvasyāpi prameyatvād abhidheyatvāc ca
children.translated_text: Here there is no negative pervasion between knowability and nameability, because everything is both knowable and nameable.

children.text: vyatirekamātravyāptikaṃ kevalavyatireki yathā pṛthivī tarebhyo bhidyate gandhavattvāt
children.translated_text: That whose pervasion is only negative is purely negative, as in: 'Earth is distinct from the others, because it has smell.'

children.text: yad itarebhyo na bhidyate na tad gandhavat
children.translated_text: Whatever is not distinct from the others is not possessed of smell.
For example, water.
And this is not so.

children.text: tasmān na tatheti atra yad gandhavat tad itarabhinnam ity anvayadṛṣṭānto nāsti pṛthivīmātrasya pakṣatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Therefore it is not so; here there is no positive example, 'whatever has smell is distinct from the others,' because earth alone is the subject.
The subject is that in which the probandum is doubtful.
For example, when smoke is the reason, the mountain.
A similar instance is that in which the probandum is certain.
For example, in that same case, the kitchen.
A dissimilar instance is that in which the absence of the probandum is certain.
For example, in that same case, the great lake.
The five fallacious reasons are the irregular, the contradictory, the counterbalanced by a valid opposite reason, the unestablished, and the contradicted.
The irregular is the inconclusive.
It is threefold.
It is divided into common, uncommon, and non-exclusive.
Among these, the common inconclusive reason is one that occurs where the probandum is absent.

children.text: yathā parvato vahnimān prameyatvād iti prameyatvasya vahnyabhāvavati hrade vidyamānatvāt
children.translated_text: For example, 'the mountain has fire because it is knowable'; knowability is present in a lake, where fire is absent.
The uncommon reason is excluded from all similar and dissimilar instances.
For example, 'sound is eternal because it is sound.'

children.text: śabdatvaṃ sarvebhyo nityebhyo'ntyebhyaś ca vyāvṛttaṃ śabdamātravṛtti
children.translated_text: Soundness, occurring only in sound, is excluded from all eternal and non-eternal things.
The non-exclusive reason is devoid of positive and negative examples.
For example, 'everything is non-eternal because it is knowable.'
Here, because everything is the subject, there is no example.
A contradictory reason is a reason pervaded by the absence of the probandum.
As in: 'sound is eternal because it is produced.'
For producedness is pervaded by the absence of eternality, that is, by non-eternality.

children.text: yasya sādhyabhāvasādhakaṃ hetvantaraṃ vidyate sa satpratipakṣaḥ
children.translated_text: That for which there is another reason proving the absence of the probandum is counterbalanced by a valid opposite reason.

children.text: yathā śabdo nityaḥ śrāvaṇatvāc chabdatvavad iti
children.translated_text: For example, 'sound is eternal because it is audible, like soundness.'
And: 'sound is non-eternal because it is an effect, like a pot.'
The unestablished is threefold.
It is the unestablished locus, the unestablished nature, and the unestablished pervadedness.

children.text: āśrayāsiddho yathā gaganāravindaṃ surabhy aravindatvāt sarojāravindavat
children.translated_text: The unestablished locus is, for example: 'a sky-lotus is fragrant because it is a lotus, like a pond-lotus.'
Here the sky-lotus is the locus.
And it simply does not exist.
The unestablished nature is, for example: 'sound is a quality because it is visible.'

children.text: atra cākṣuṣatvaṃ śabde nāsti śabdasya śrāvaṇatvāt
children.translated_text: Here visibility does not exist in sound, because sound is audible.
The unestablished pervadedness is that which is conditioned by an adjunct.
An adjunct is that which, while pervading the probandum, does not pervade the means of proof.
Pervasion of the probandum is the state of not being the counterpositive of an absolute absence located in the same substratum as the probandum.
Non-pervasion of the means is being the counterpositive of a desired absolute absence in what possesses the means.

children.text: parvato dhūmavān vahnimattvād ity atrārdrendhanasaṃyoga upādhiḥ
children.translated_text: In the argument 'the mountain has smoke because it has fire,' contact with wet fuel is the adjunct.
For so it is.
'Where there is smoke, there is contact with wet fuel' is pervasion of the probandum.
'Where there is fire, there is absence of contact with wet fuel' is non-pervasion of the means.

children.text: evaṃ sādhyavyāpakatve sati sādhanāvyāpakatvād ārdrendhanasaṃyoga upādhiḥ
children.translated_text: Thus, because it pervades the probandum while not pervading the means, contact with wet fuel is an adjunct.
Because it is accompanied by an adjunct, the possession of fire has unestablished pervadedness.

children.text: yasya sādhyābhāvaḥ pramāṇāntareṇa niścitaḥ sa bādhitaḥ
children.translated_text: That for which the absence of the probandum is ascertained by another means of knowledge is contradicted.
For example: 'fire is not hot because it is a substance.'

children.text: atrānuṣṇatvaṃ sādhyaṃ tadabhāva uṣṇatvaṃ spārśanapratyakṣeṇa gṛhyata iti bādhitatvam ||
children.translated_text: Here non-hotness is the probandum; its absence, heat, is apprehended by tactile perception, and so there is contradiction.
Comparison is the instrument of analogical knowledge.
Analogical knowledge is knowledge of the relation between a name and the named thing.
The instrument for that is cognition of similarity.
Remembering the meaning of an instructional sentence is the intermediate operation.

children.text: tathā hi kaścid gavayaśabdārtham ajānan kutaścid āraṇyakapuruṣād gosadṛśo gavaya iti śrutvā vanaṃ gato vākyārthaṃ smaran gosadṛśaṃ piṇḍaṃ paśyati
children.translated_text: Thus, someone who does not know the meaning of the word 'gavaya,' having heard from some forest-dweller that a gavaya is similar to a cow, goes to the forest and, remembering the meaning of the sentence, sees an object similar to a cow.

children.text: tadanantaram asau gavayaśabdavācya ity upamitir utpadyate ||
children.translated_text: Immediately afterward the analogical cognition arises: 'this is what is denoted by the word gavaya.'
Verbal testimony is the statement of a trustworthy person.
A trustworthy person is one who speaks what is true.
A sentence is a collection of words.
For example, 'bring the cow.'
A word is that which has semantic capacity.

children.text: asmāt padād ayam artho boddhavya itīśvarasaṃketaḥ śaktiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Semantic capacity is God's convention that 'this meaning is to be understood from this word.'
Expectancy, semantic fitness, and proximity are the causes of knowledge of sentence-meaning.
Expectancy is a word's incapacity to convey a syntactic connection when separated from another word.
Semantic fitness is non-contradiction of meaning.
Proximity is the utterance of the words without delay.
A sentence lacking expectancy and the like is not a valid means of knowledge.

children.text: yathā gaur aśvaḥ puruṣo hastīti na pramāṇam ākāṅkṣāvirahāt
children.translated_text: For example, "a cow, a horse, a man, an elephant" is not a means of knowledge, because expectancy is absent.

children.text: agninā siñced iti na pramāṇaṃ yogyatāvirahāt
children.translated_text: "One should sprinkle with fire" is not a means of knowledge, because semantic fitness is absent.

children.text: prahare prehare 'sahoccāritāni gām ānayetyādipadāni na pramāṇaṃ saṃnidhyabhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: Words such as "bring the cow," when uttered at intervals of a watch each, are not a means of knowledge, because proximity is absent.
A sentence is of two kinds.
It is Vedic and worldly.
The Vedic sentence, because it is spoken by the Lord, is entirely a means of knowledge.
But a worldly sentence, when spoken by a trustworthy person, is a means of knowledge.
Anything else is not a means of knowledge.
Knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is verbal knowledge.
Its instrument is verbal testimony.
Non-veridical experience is threefold, divided as doubt, error, and suppositional reasoning.
Doubt is cognition, with regard to one substrate, that apprehends it as qualified by several mutually opposed properties.
For example, "Is it a post, or is it a man?"
False cognition is error.
For example, "This is silver" in mother-of-pearl.

children.text: vyāpyāropeṇa vyāpakāropas tarkaḥ yathā yadi vahnir na syāt tarhi dhūmo'pi na syād iti ||
children.translated_text: <s>Tarka</s> (suppositional reasoning) is the superimposition of the pervader through the superimposition of the pervaded, as in: "If there were no fire, then there would also be no smoke."
Memory too is of two kinds.
It is veridical and non-veridical; that produced by valid cognition is veridical.
That produced by invalid cognition is non-veridical.
Pleasure is what is experienced as agreeable to all.
Pain is what is experienced as disagreeable to all.
Desire is wish.
Anger is aversion.
Action-producing effort is exertion.
<s>Dharma</s> is that which is produced by prescribed action.
But <s>adharma</s> is that which is produced by prohibited action.
The eight beginning with cognition are special qualities belonging only to the self.
Cognition, desire, and effort are of two kinds.
They are eternal and non-eternal.
The eternal ones belong to the Lord.
The non-eternal ones belong to the individual soul.
<s>Saṃskāra</s> (dispositional trace) is threefold.
It is impetus, latent impression, and elasticity.
Impetus occurs in the four beginning with earth and in mind.
Latent impression, produced by experience and a cause of memory, occurs only in the self.

children.text: anyathā kṛtasya punas tadavasthāpādakaḥ sthitisthāpakaḥ kaṭādipṛthivīvṛttiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Elasticity is that which restores something altered to that very condition again, and it occurs in earthly things such as a mat.
Motion is action whose nature is movement.
Throwing upward is the cause of conjunction with an upper region.
Throwing downward is the cause of conjunction with a lower region.
Contraction is the cause of conjunction close to the body.
Expansion is the cause of conjunction distant from it.
Everything else is locomotion.
It occurs only in the four beginning with earth and in mind.
A universal is eternal, one, and recurrent in many things.
It occurs in substance, quality, and action.
It is twofold, divided into higher and lower.
The higher is existence.
The lower is such things as substanceness.
Particularities are differentiators that occur in eternal substances.
Inherence is an eternal relation.
It occurs in things that are inseparably established.

children.text: yayor dvayor madhya ekam avinaśyadaparāśritam evāvatiṣṭhate tāv ayutasiddhau
children.translated_text: Of two things, when one remains only as dependent on the other, so long as that other has not perished, those two are inseparably established.

children.text: yathāvayavāvayavinau guṇaguṇinau kriyākriyāvantau jātivyaktī viśeṣanityadravye ceti ||
children.translated_text: Examples are part and whole, quality and qualified substance, action and possessor of action, universal and individual, and particularity and eternal substance.
Prior absence is beginningless and has an end.
It is the absence of an effect before its production.
Destruction is with a beginning and endless.
It is the absence of an effect after its production.
Absolute absence has a counterpositive delimited by relation in all three times.
For example, "There is no pot on the ground."

children.text: tādātmyasaṃbandhāvacchinnapratiyogitāko 'nyonyābhāvaḥ yathā ghaṭaḥ paṭo na bhavatīti ||
children.translated_text: Mutual absence has a counterpositive delimited by the relation of identity, as in: "A pot is not a cloth."

children.text: sarveṣāṃ padārthānāṃ yathāyatham ukteṣv antarbhāvāt saptaiva padārthā iti siddham ||
children.translated_text: Since all entities are included, each as appropriate, in the categories stated above, it is established that there are exactly seven categories.
For the accomplishment of instruction for children in the doctrines of <s>Kaṇāda</s> and <s>Nyāya</s>,
the <s>Tarkasaṃgraha</s> was composed by the learned <s>Annambhaṭṭa</s>.
